description: Width tiers for Visual Arts — Years 3–4
subject: Visual Arts

width_notes.minimum: The narrowest single task context that honestly meets the descriptor's command term. For Years 3–4, minimum is one making or exploring act that uses visual conventions with communicative intent.
width_notes.typical: Full descriptor scope as intended — multiple materials, contexts and purposes; emerging deliberate composition and reflection.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment through additional cultural contexts, art forms, collaborative modes or cross-curricular connections. Adds new contexts, not higher difficulty.

AC9AVA4C01.minimum_width: Use at least two visual conventions and one visual arts process with chosen materials to create an artwork that communicates one idea, perspective or meaning.
AC9AVA4C01.typical_width: Use combinations of visual conventions, processes and materials to plan and create artworks that intentionally communicate ideas and perspectives; make compositional choices (foreground/background, tone, scale); document reasoning for choices.
wider: Create a visual artwork inspired by a performance work (dance, drama) — communicate the lines, movement and gestures observed through abstract or representational means
Explore how an illustrator communicates perspective and story in a familiar text; apply a similar approach to communicate a specific point of view in your own artwork

Investigate and apply compositional techniques used by artists from a specific cultural tradition, including First Nations Australian visual arts — with guidance from culturally authoritative resources, explore how composition communicates meaning
elaborations: drawing on a selection of topics they may be exploring in other subjects, mind-mapping some ideas that link to these topics, using Viewpoints to explore multiple possibilities such as,
, extending the ideas to arrive at 3 compositional ideas, selecting one idea, documenting their reasons for the selection and making the artwork

exploring tools and awareness of measured and freeform perspectives; for example, using digital and/or analog tools to reference a special place near their school, and dividing the scene, surface or paper into foreground, middle ground and background sections to consider how to create depth in their artwork

creating a visual artwork inspired by a performance that can become a part of the performance or the setting for a situation; for example, creating an abstract painting that documents the lines, movement and gestures in a dance, or illustrating a scene from a devised drama

considering how as artists they can communicate perspectives to viewers through the use of visual conventions and visual arts processes in the way that an illustrator represents ideas in a text to communicate aspects of the story, and applying this to their own work

using Viewpoints to develop questions as they experiment with composition to arrange visual conventions, subject matter and materials based on a designated area and deliberately changing the meaning of a visual story

combining their understanding of visual conventions and visual arts processes to create different meaning in an artwork; for example, using a range of 2D media such as charcoal and coloured pastels to create gradation of tone in their artwork

AC9AVA4D01.minimum_width: Experiment with at least one combination of materials or processes; document what was tried and what was noticed.
AC9AVA4D01.typical_width: Experiment with a range of materials, processes and combinations; explore how artists use composition (space, balance, foreground/background); document thinking with annotations and Viewpoints questions; reflect on outcomes.
wider: Explore visual conventions, symbols or patterns used by First Nations Australian artists, with guidance from community representatives or culturally authoritative resources
Investigate how artists work collaboratively — analyse a collaboratively produced artwork and discuss why artists might choose this mode; apply a collaborative approach in a class work
Explore printmaking processes (e.g. multiple-print colour experiments, cutting and combining prints with 2D media) to investigate how repetition and variation produce visual effects
elaborations: exploring the ways that artists use composition by observing space and balance within an artwork; for example, using transparent material or digital tools layered over a diverse selection of artworks to outline the dominant forms and divisions of space
exploring materials based on visual conventions; for example, creating a tactile (texture) board from a collection of materials and objects, brainstorming adjectives to describe the textures
working within limits to explore and experiment with the properties of materials; for example, playing a game to find different ways of creating lines with a wide range of materials in a timed period

learning to use visual arts language when describing and documenting their thinking and learning; for example, developing questions based on Viewpoints, and using arrows and short statements to annotate their visual experiments

manipulating and experimenting with combinations of various materials and technologies to create visual effects; for example, using crosshatching to create tone, or using design elements to focus the viewer's attention on a composition

AC9AVA4E01.minimum_width: Explore one artwork from a different culture, time or place; make one observation about what it is made of or what it might communicate.
AC9AVA4E01.typical_width: Explore a range of artworks created across cultures, times and places; compare how artists' contexts affect their approaches to similar themes; investigate artists' practices through their own accounts; identify visual features, purposes and meanings.
wider: Explore artworks by First Nations Australian artists that communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — use Viewpoints questions to investigate what artworks teach about the subject matter

Find and compare artworks addressing the same theme (e.g. sustainability, community) by artists from different cultural contexts — identify similarities and differences in approach, materials and purpose

Examine cultural works in the school environment (murals, memorials, architectural features, displays) — categorise them by purpose (social, decorative, functional, cultural) and discuss who they serve
elaborations: exploring a diverse range of artworks created by artists working collaboratively and brainstorming the reasons why artists might choose to work as a team
exploring artists' practice by sourcing information created or co-created by the artist and using Viewpoints to develop questions to develop understanding of the practices
observing and exploring details such as use of materials, patterns, proportions or familiar features in artworks

making connections and comparisons between artists working across cultures, times and/or places; for example, finding similarities and differences between the ways that an artist's context impacts their approach to a theme such as sustainability or community celebrations
exploring ways to represent the world as they see it; for example, using ideas and experience about a recent event
identifying ways that artworks by different artists can present multiple perspectives of the same event and discussing how these works can develop social awareness
describing and categorising visual features and cultural works around the school according to their purpose; for example, social, decorative, architectural, functional, cultural

AC9AVA4E02.minimum_width: Explore one example of a First Nations Australian artwork or cultural expression that communicates connection to Country/Place; share one observation about what it communicates.
AC9AVA4E02.typical_width: Explore how First Nations Australian artists use visual arts to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place; access artists' own accounts; investigate symbols, emblems and their cultural importance with guidance from people with cultural authority.
wider: Explore artworks that share cultural accounts of Country/Place — examine visual conventions, symbols and patterns with representatives of a First Nations Australian community or through co-created resources
Use Viewpoints questions to map your own cultural connections (place, language, family customs, values) and create an artwork that communicates your personal connection to place
Investigate the diversity of First Nations Nations and their distinct cultural expressions — examine artworks to learn about identity, stories and communities
elaborations: looking at visual artworks that represent the importance of Country/Place and Story for First Nations Australians as a starting point for talking about different ways of seeing the same place and telling stories
accessing examples of contemporary First Nations Australian artists' ideas about Country/Place through cultural expressions
examining a diverse range of symbols and emblems and learning from people with cultural authority about their importance to First Nations Australians' identity and culture
exploring topics in other learning areas, such as the diversity of Nations, by examining a diverse range of cultural expressions or artworks of and by First Nations Australian artists
considering what their own cultural connections are as individuals; for example, considering place, language, family customs, values and beliefs
exploring visual conventions, symbols or patterns with representatives of a First Nations Australian community, or resources that are created or co-created by First Nations Australians

AC9AVA4P01.minimum_width: Share at least one example from their visual arts practice in an informal setting; explain one decision or idea behind the work.
AC9AVA4P01.typical_width: Share and/or display artworks and visual arts practice in informal settings; select examples to communicate development of ideas; present in multiple formats (folio, peer circle, digital platform, physical display); produce artist statements in written or spoken form.
wider: Trial different presentation contexts — adapt a physical wall display for a digital platform, considering what needs to change and why
Create a multimedia artist statement that pairs documentation of the making process with an explanation of ideas and meanings
Develop and present a work-in-progress review to peers — identify choices made so far, explain what is working and what might change
elaborations: selecting examples from their visual arts practice (for example, experimentation with materials and processes or different compositional approaches for a final artwork) and arranging these in a visual display to share the development of their ideas

deciding on appropriate ways to share their artworks and their learning; for example, including experiments and self-reflections in folios or visual diaries for assessment, demonstrating progress being made via peer circle shares in class

trialling different ways of presenting artworks in different locations; for example, presenting a school wall display of artworks, considering what might need to change so that it can be shared on a digital platform
discussing and documenting the ideas, themes and meaning/s of their artwork; for example, taking the form of a written or spoken artist statement
identifying and explaining their own and other artists' choices in art-making, including visual arts processes, visual conventions and materials
